result.title: Dissimilarity-Based Markov Decision Processes for Stabilizing State Distributions
result.comment: 44 pages, 12 figures, 13 tables. Xun Shen, Yuepeng Wang, and Daniyal Sajedi-Hosseini contributed equally. Under review at TMLR
result.summary: Reinforcement learning for stochastic systems typically optimizes expected cumulative rewards, while reliable and repeatable behavior also depends on how the state distribution evolves over time. Optimizing expected return alone does not guarantee that this distribution converges to a desired target or remains stable. This paper develops a theoretical framework for learning policies that stabilize state distributions. We formulate the problem as a Dissimilarity-based Markov Decision Process (DMDP), in which the policy acts on the current state distribution and the objective measures its dissimilarity to a target distribution. We establish sufficient conditions under which the optimal policy makes the target distribution asymptotically stable. To support policy learning, we introduce a finite-dimensional representation of distributions and show how stability guarantees for its parameter dynamics extend to the underlying state distributions. We further develop certificates for the learned policies, including their deployment using estimated distribution parameters. These results quantify how learning and estimation errors affect the guarantees and identify conditions under which learned policies retain asymptotic stability. For practical implementation, we combine distribution estimates and target-dependent rewards with PPO and SAC. A computable example on a linear system illustrates the proposed theoretical certificates. Furthermore, experiments on a HalfCheetah task demonstrate the benefits of distribution feedback and explicit target matching for regulating the velocity distribution.

AI.brief_summary: 提出以不相似度衡量当前状态分布与目标分布差距的 DMDP 框架，学习使目标分布渐近稳定的策略，并给出有限维分布表示、稳定性充分条件与部署证书，结合 PPO/SAC 验证。
AI.relevance_reason: 其状态分布的收敛与稳定性证书，可能为分析 loop/迭代式 latent 推理中内部状态分布是否漂移或收敛提供核查线索，但与视觉推理本身无直接关联。
